rotation_dimension: quantitative-methods expert (Zira) vs. human-centered interpreter (David) - Zira holds the technical-expert side for this paper

speaker_a.persona: Human-centered AI / HCI interpreter. Explains fairness stakes, study design as it touches people, and real-world consequences in plain language; presses on what the numbers mean for actual users. Asks and explains in equal measure.

speaker_b.persona: Evaluation-methods and statistics expert. Owns the technical machinery - tau-Bench, pass rates, expected calibration error, GEE models - and explains it intuition-first; skeptical of overclaiming. Asks and explains in equal measure.

lines.text: Welcome back. Today we're digging into a paper called Lost in Simulation: LLM-Simulated Users are Unreliable Proxies for Human Users in Agentic Evaluations, by Preethi Seshadri, Samuel Cahyawijaya, Ayomide Odumakinde, Sameer Singh, and Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant, out of UC Irvine and Cohere, 2026.

And the title is basically the whole thesis. Agentic benchmarks increasingly rely on LLM-simulated users to scalably evaluate agent performance, but the robustness, validity, and fairness of that entire approach have never really been examined.
Wait, so when a benchmark tests how well an agent handles something like a customer service conversation, the customer on the other end is often just another AI pretending to be a person?
Exactly. These benchmarks simulate the conversation between an LLM agent and a user, and the user is itself an LLM. It's cheaper and it scales, so it's become the default setup.
But has anyone actually checked whether that stand-in behaves anything like a real person would?

Apparently not, and that's exactly the gap this paper closes. The authors ran a user study with real participants across the United States, India, Kenya, and Nigeria, to test whether LLM-simulated users are reliable proxies for real human users on tau-Bench retail tasks.
Four countries is a serious sample. What did they find?

First problem: the simulation isn't even robust to itself. Agent success rates swing by up to 9 percentage points depending on which LLM plays the user. If the grader disagrees with itself that much, what does that mean for someone trying to trust these leaderboard numbers?

It means the score depends on which fake customer you happen to draw, which is shaky ground for deciding an agent's ready to ship. What about matching real humans, not just agreeing with other simulators?
That's the miscalibration finding. Evaluations using simulated users systematically underestimate agent performance on the most challenging tasks, and overestimate it on moderately difficult ones.
So simulated evals make agents look worse exactly where the task is hardest, and look better right in the messy middle. That's the opposite of reassuring.

It gets more pointed. African American Vernacular English speakers experience consistently worse success rates and worse calibration errors than Standard American English speakers, and those disparities compound significantly with age.

So this isn't just noise in the measurement, it's a fairness problem. If the evaluation itself treats speech communities unevenly, a system that passes the benchmark could still be quietly failing the users who most need it to work.

Right, and it's not only AAVE speakers. Simulated users turn out to be a differentially effective proxy across populations generally, performing worst for AAVE and Indian English speakers specifically. On top of that, simulated users introduce their own conversational artifacts and surface different failure patterns than human users do.

Which is why the authors frame this as bigger than a leaderboard quirk. Current evaluation practice risks misrepresenting what agents can actually do across different user populations, and can obscure real-world deployment challenges until it's too late.
That's the abstract. So why does it even matter this much whether agents handle sustained, multi-turn conversation instead of one-shot question and answer? What goes wrong if they don't?

Because agents for everyday tasks like travel reservations, order management, and appointment scheduling are everywhere now, and a static, single-turn test just doesn't capture what they actually have to do in a real interaction.

Right, so benchmarks evolved toward sustained, context-aware, multi-turn interaction, agents conversing naturally, following policies and instructions, making the right tool calls across many turns. To automate that at scale, the field simulates the user with an LLM too.

The paper actually shows that gap directly. There's a Figure 1 with side-by-side conversation snippets, a simulated user and a human user on the exact same task, and the simulated user asks more questions and comes across as noticeably more polite.
So if even a two-line snippet gives it away, doesn't that call into question whether automated evaluation alone can be trusted here?

That's exactly why the authors say relying on a single user simulation model is risky, results may just vary across different user LLMs, that's the robustness concern. And without checking against actual people, you can't know if simulated interactions really predict what happens with real ones.

There's a third piece too: these evaluations tend to treat users as one homogeneous group, when people actually vary widely in formality, verbosity, politeness norms, and linguistic background. Simulated users might approximate some populations far better than others, which is exactly the fairness risk.
Wait, did prior work ever actually validate any of this against real people before now?

No, that's precisely the gap. The authors boil it down to three questions: robustness, how consistent are evaluations across different user simulation LLMs; validity, do simulated users reliably proxy real human users; and fairness, does simulation represent some user groups better than others.

And using tau-Bench retail tasks as their case study, they confirm all three concerns are real: simulation lacks robustness, and it systematically misestimates performance compared to human users, underestimating success on the hardest tasks while overestimating outcomes on moderately difficult scenarios, on top of the demographic bias and conversational artifacts we already covered.

Next time, let's get into how they actually pulled this off, running tau-Bench retail tasks with real participants recruited across those four countries, and what it took to fairly compare a human against an LLM standing in for one.
So, how did they actually run this study? Before we get there, let's place it against what came before, because that shelf is thin.

Right, other work has poked at user simulation before, in math tutoring and daily planning, but mostly asking whether a simulated user behaves believably or sounds polite, Turing-test style. One group even found real deviations between simulated and actual shopping actions.

But notice what none of them did: nobody checked whether results hold up across different simulator models, and nobody asked whether simulation treats every user group the same. That's the gap this paper steps into.

There's a second, separate thread too, from the broader NLP fairness literature. Annotator studies keep finding that judgments of toxicity or safety split along race, gender, and political lines, and language models themselves have been shown to lean Western, wealthy, and English-speaking in whose opinions they reflect.

Including aligning more with White annotators than Black or Asian annotators on something as basic as politeness judgments. So this paper is really asking: does that same skew show up when an LLM isn't judging text, but playing the user inside an agent evaluation?
Nobody had tested that directly. Okay, onto the actual test bed then. What is tau-Bench, for anyone who hasn't run into it?

It's a widely-used benchmark for agentic tool use, built around customer service scenarios. An agent and a user LLM converse, the user has private task instructions with a goal, and the agent has to make tool calls against a realistic database while following policy.
And success is strict, right? Not just did the conversation go smoothly.

Strict on two counts. The final database state has to exactly match the one correct outcome, and the agent's replies have to convey every piece of information the task required, checked automatically against ground-truth text. tau-Bench ships 115 retail tasks and 50 airline tasks total.
This paper only uses the retail side. Why narrow it down like that?

To get systematic coverage within one domain instead of spreading thin across two. They also scrub the task instructions so nothing hints at a user's identity or expected behavior, so that can't contaminate the comparison later.

Here's the clever bit, though. tau-Bench doesn't ship difficulty labels, so they invented one: ran the whole benchmark five times with GPT-4o as both agent and simulated user, and counted how often each task succeeded, which naturally sorts tasks into six difficulty buckets, zero out of five up to five out of five. Then they picked three tasks per bucket, eighteen total, so every difficulty level gets equal weight.
Now here's where I get interested, because this is the part that's actually about people. They recruited participants from the United States, India, Kenya, and Nigeria. Why those four?
You'd know better than me, what's the reasoning there?

tau-Bench tasks are English-only, so they needed countries with large English-speaking populations, but still wanted geographic and linguistic spread rather than only testing English speakers in English-speaking countries. Prolific handled recruiting everywhere except Nigeria, where platform coverage was too thin, so they used snowball sampling there instead.
And how much did each person actually do?

Four tasks apiece, drawn randomly from that pool of eighteen, two from the harder end and two from the easier end, all against the same GPT-4o agent, roughly thirty-five to forty minutes total. The part I really want to flag: for US participants specifically, they screened for two groups on purpose, White Standard American English speakers and Black African American Vernacular English speakers, since those are the groups AI fairness research keeps coming back to.
Age-stratified too, on top of that?

Yes, three US age bands, eighteen to thirty-four, thirty-five to fifty-four, and fifty-five plus, since prior research says tech familiarity shifts a lot with age. Outside the US they could only recruit the youngest band, purely due to who was available on the ground.

Now, the metrics, because this is where the paper turns all that recruiting into a real comparison. Success rate is the easy one, just the percentage of tasks completed correctly, same automated grading whether the user was a person or a simulated LLM.
And the harder one, expected calibration error, ECE for short? I've only heard that term from probability forecasting, not user studies.

Right, normally ECE checks whether a model's confidence scores match reality. Here it's borrowed in spirit: instead of confidence versus outcome, it's simulated-user success rate versus human-user success rate at each difficulty level, weighted by how many real human attempts landed in that bucket. Bigger gap, worse calibration, and zero would mean the simulation is a perfect stand-in for real people.
So it's not just are simulated users worse, it's are they wrong in a lopsided way, underselling agents on the hard stuff and overselling them on the medium stuff.

That's exactly the shape they find, and it sets up everything next. Coming up, we get into how robust these numbers actually are across different simulator models, and how well simulation holds up as a stand-in for the real people they just recruited.
Okay, let's dive right into the results, starting with robustness. They held the agent fixed at GPT-4o and only changed which model played the simulated user.
And that alone was enough to move the numbers?

It was. Three of the five user models, GPT-4o, Sonnet 3.7, and Kimi-K2-Thinking, land in a cluster, roughly 67 to 71 percent success rates. But swap in Sonnet 4.5 as the user, and you get almost a 9 percentage point gap versus Sonnet 3.7.
So the agent didn't change at all, just who's simulating the customer, and the score can swing by 9 points. What does that do to something like a leaderboard comparison?
It undermines it. If two teams each report a single number using a different simulated-user model, those numbers aren't really comparable, even when the underlying agent is identical.
I'd have guessed the fix is simple, just pick the strongest available model to play the user and you're covered.

You'd think so, but the data argues against it. Sonnet 3.7 is generally considered the stronger model, yet using GPT-4o as the user model produced a slightly higher success rate, 67.8 versus 67.0, and a much tighter standard deviation, 1.2 versus 3.3.
So the so-called weaker model actually gave a more stable read on the agent.
Right, which points to something other than raw capability. It looks like closeness between the agent and user model matters more than either one being the single strongest option on its own.
That's a real design implication for anyone building an eval. The user model isn't a neutral instrument, it's a variable you have to control for.
So what's actually at stake if a lab just publishes one leaderboard number without disclosing which model played the user?
Anyone downstream trusting that number to pick an agent for production. They'd be comparing apples to oranges without knowing it.

And doesn't that make it hard to trust the big jumps at face value too? They flag that it's genuinely difficult to tell whether Sonnet 4.5's jump as a user model reflects real capability gains or just that model having seen more of this kind of benchmark during training.

Fair, that contamination question is impossible to fully rule out from outside the lab. Okay, that's robustness. Now the paper pivots to validity, forget consistency across user models, are simulated users even tracking real human behavior?

Right, and they pick the friendliest possible test first. Prior work shows LLMs carry a strong Western, Anglocentric bias, so the logic is, if simulated users are going to match anyone well, it should be US participants.
So this is the best case scenario for the simulators, not a stress test.
Exactly, they're checking calibration in the setting where they'd expect the strongest alignment between simulated and human users.
And even in the best case?

Even there, agents only hit a 45.2 percent success rate with real US participants, and the calibration error between human and simulated users comes out to 15.1. That's substantial miscalibration in the most favorable setting they could construct.

Figure 2 is the picture of that, human success rate plotted against success rate with the simulated users for the US group, with that 15.1 calibration error and error bars at plus or minus one standard deviation.
And the miscalibration isn't spread evenly across task difficulty. It's worst at the first and fourth difficulty bins, where the calibration error jumps to 25.9 across just those two.
Which direction does it break in? Does the simulation make agents look better or worse than they really are?

Both, depending on where you look. On the hardest tasks it undersells the agent, human success there was 30.8 percent, and the simulated evaluation reads lower. On the moderately difficult tasks it flips and overestimates, human success there was 39.0 percent.
So an agent could look artificially weak on the hard tasks and artificially strong on the medium ones, in the same benchmark, at the same time.
If it's this skewed even in the friendliest test case, what does that mean for people actually deciding which agent to ship based on these scores?

It means the number on the leaderboard could be quietly wrong in either direction, and you wouldn't know which. And apparently this is just the calibration story averaged across everyone. Next part digs into who this fails hardest for, the fairness findings are coming, and from the sound of it, that's where it gets uncomfortable.
Last part ended on a tease: who does this simulation gap actually fail hardest? Turns out there's a whole section for that, and it's literally titled Fairness.

They split the US sample by dialect, Standard American English, SAE, versus African American Vernacular English, AAVE, and by age group, then widened out to three non-Western countries: India, Kenya, and Nigeria.
Before I get into the model, David, what's actually at stake for someone speaking AAVE and getting an agent that's both worse-performing and worse at knowing it's worse?

That combination is the dangerous part. It's not just a worse experience, it's a worse experience the evaluation itself doesn't flag as worse. Someone gets a rougher interaction, and the numbers underneath it say everything's fine.
So how big is this, statistically?

Overall US success was 45.2 percent with an ECE Human-LLM of 15.1, Expected Calibration Error, meaning how far the simulated user's read on success drifts from what a real human actually experienced. A Generalized Estimating Equations model, GEE for short, controlling for age, education, AI experience, AI usage, and task difficulty, found the dialect disparity statistically significant: beta 0.61, p less than 0.001. SAE participants: 50.6 percent success, 11.7 ECE. AAVE participants: 39.4 percent success, 20.3 ECE.

That's an 11.2 point drop in success rate and an 8.6 point jump in calibration error, just from dialect. And the paper doesn't hedge on what that could mean: real disparities in the quality of retail assistance people get, and in how easy the interaction feels.
And it gets worse with age, doesn't it? What does that trend actually look like for someone who's been dealing with this system longer?

It does. SAE success actually ticks up slightly with age, about 3 points from the 18 to 34 group to the 55-plus group. AAVE goes the opposite way, a 7.6 point drop over that same span. The group already worse off keeps sliding as they get older.
What does that look like in the actual table?

Table 2. SAE by age: 49.2 percent at 18 to 34, 52.2 at 35 to 54, 52.1 at 55-plus, calibration error staying in the 11 to 14 range throughout. AAVE by age: 41.0 percent at 18 to 34, 39.9 at 35 to 54, then down to 33.4 percent at 55-plus. Calibration error there moves from 18.9 up to 21.6 at 35 to 54, then eases slightly to 20.5 at 55-plus.

And it's confirmed statistically. Nearly a 12 point gap between SAE and AAVE at 35 to 54, almost 19 points by 55-plus. Age-stratified GEE effects: beta 0.67, p 0.01 at 35 to 54; beta 1.24, p 0.001 at 55-plus.
How solid is that calibration story specifically? Is it the same shape of miscalibration at every age, or does it look different?

Different shape, not just bigger. The calibration gap peaks at 35 to 54, a 10.3 point ECE difference. Figure 3 shows SAE miscalibration concentrated mostly in one difficulty bin, while AAVE miscalibration shows up across every bin.
Does a decent success rate mean the calibration is fine too, then?

No, that's the trap. They don't move together. SAE participants 18 to 34 have both a lower success rate and a lower calibration error. SAE participants 55-plus have both a higher success rate and a higher calibration error. Fixing one doesn't fix the other.
Okay, that's the US story. What happens when they widen out to India, Kenya, and Nigeria?

They narrow that comparison to the 18 to 34 group, just for participant-availability reasons. The spread there is much smaller than what we just walked through, success rates ranging from 41.0 to 49.2 percent, nowhere near the dialect and age gaps inside the US.
Kenya and Nigeria basically landed on top of each other, didn't they?
Yeah, 43.5 percent and 43.7 percent. And a GEE model confirms none of the cross-country differences are statistically significant, every p-value above 0.49.
But David, here's the part that should bother you more than the success-rate numbers. What do you make of the calibration side?

Simulated users are best calibrated to SAE participants, ECE of 13.0, and worst calibrated to AAVE and Indian participants, both at 18.9. Full spread: SAE 49.2 percent and 13.0 ECE, AAVE 41.0 percent and 18.9, India 46.2 percent and 18.9, Kenya 43.5 percent and 15.6, Nigeria 43.7 percent and 17.6.
India's success rate isn't the lowest in that table, but the simulation is just as unreliable there as it is for AAVE speakers. Two very different populations, failed by the same blind spot.

One more wrinkle: across countries, calibration is strongest on moderately hard tasks, the 20 to 40 percent difficulty range, but it consistently overestimates performance on easy tasks, the 80 to 100 percent bins, shown in Figure 4.
So evaluations leaning on simulated users risk underselling how hard these tasks actually are once you deploy to a genuinely diverse, global user base.

Which is a good place to stop and ask the harder question. We know where the reliability breaks and who it breaks for. Next part, we get into what's actually going wrong inside these conversations that produces it.
Okay, so last part we left off asking what's actually going wrong inside these conversations. Let's open that up. Section 4.4 looks at interaction structure and content.
Structurally, are simulated and human conversations even comparable? Or is this apples to oranges from the start?

Surface level, they're pretty similar. Number of turns, number of actions, words per turn, all comparable between simulated and human user interactions. The differences show up when you look at content.
Content meaning what people actually say, not just how much of it.

Right. Take question-asking. Simulated user conversations include questions in 18.8% of user turns and 51.8% of agent turns. Human users only ask questions 9.8% of the time, though their agents ask questions more, 56.3%.
So simulated users are almost twice as curious as real ones. That's backwards from what I'd have guessed, real users navigating an unfamiliar agent should be the ones asking more.
And it's not uniform across human users either. Nigerian participants ask questions in only 4.3% of turns, well below the human average.
That's a real behavioral texture that a simulated user just isn't going to reproduce. What about politeness, please, thank you, apologizing, that kind of thing?

That gap is even bigger. Simulated conversations show politeness indicators in 39.2% of user turns and 52.0% of agent turns. Human conversations: 19.9% and 41.1%. And the paper's explicit that the simulated-versus-human gap is larger than any gap they see among different human subgroups.
So simulated users perform a kind of exaggerated politeness that doesn't track how any actual demographic talks to an agent. That's a specific, fixable-sounding miscalibration.
It is partially fixable, actually. They tried prompting simulated users to limit politeness, and that intervention did alter calibration patterns and shrink the gap for the most miscalibrated groups.

Good, so it's not hopeless, you can nudge the simulator toward realism if you know where to look. Let's get into the errors section, because that's the part I actually care about as an HCI person, what breaks and for whom.

They break errors into four types: argument errors, where the agent takes the right action with wrong arguments, missing action errors, extra action errors, and output errors, where the expected output is missing or wrong.
And do simulated and human conversations produce the same mix of those errors?
Not quite. Argument errors happen 32.2% of the time with simulated users, versus a range of 23.2% to 45.8% across human groups, with AAVE participants experiencing the highest rate.
That range across human groups alone is a fairness flag, before you even bring simulated users into it.
Agreed. But then missing and extra action errors actually run lower for simulated users: 17.8% versus 15.8% to 25.3% for missing actions, 5.6% versus 7.6% to 13.3% for extra actions.
So agents look more competent, more efficient, when they're talking to a simulated user.

Until you hit output errors, where the pattern flips. Agents omit or produce incorrect outputs 31.4% of the time with simulated users, compared to 12.2% to 23.6% for human users. That's the reverse direction from the action errors.

So agents act more cleanly with simulated users but talk back to them worse. That's a strange split, it's like the agent handles the mechanics fine but garbles the communication layer specifically for the fake user.
That's exactly their read too, agents behave differently with simulated versus human users. More complete, efficient action sequences, but more frequent output errors.
Okay, so who gets blamed when things go wrong, the agent or the user? That feels like the crux for anyone designing these systems.

This is where it gets sharp. Looking at manually annotated error attribution for failed tasks, agents are responsible for the failure 48.9% of the time in simulated conversations, versus only 24.5% in human conversations.
So in the simulated world, it's mostly the agent's fault. What's happening on the human side, then?

Users are the primary source of failure in human conversations, 62.2%, compared to 40% in simulated ones. There's also a small "both" and "other" category on each side, but that user-versus-agent flip is the headline.

That's a big deal for anyone reading simulated-user evals as a signal about agent quality. If real users are generating most of their own friction, error attribution and error mix, and this was manually annotated and matched on task difficulty, so it's not just noise, evaluating only on simulated users hides where the actual failures come from.
Which raises the obvious next question. If we know all this is broken, what's the field actually supposed to do about it? That's next.
Last part ended on the tease: what should the field actually do about this? David, if the user side of evaluation has been this broken, where does human-centered evaluation even go from here?

It starts with taking the finding at face value. The user component has been overlooked even though equitable performance across different people is the whole point of shipping these systems. So step one is dropping the assumption that the user side is a solved variable.

Which is why their concrete asks are so modest. Benchmark robustness across multiple simulator models, validate against demographically diverse human data when it's feasible, and be transparent about simulation's limits instead of burying them.
Transparent how? Disclose it in a footnote, or actually change what gets published as the headline number?

More the former in their framing, but the stakes are the same either way. A system can look robust in the benchmark and still fail disproportionately for real users whose communication style the simulator never represented.
Because the excess politeness and question-asking we've tracked all episode are one communication norm standing in for everyone's.
Right, and a team that only validates against that norm might be optimizing for something that diverges from actual real-world use. Their phrase, not mine.
Let's get into what they admit themselves. How blunt is the Limitations section, really?

Pretty blunt. Everything here is English-only, though that just replicates a limitation already baked into the benchmarks they built on, so we don't know how any of this plays out in another language. The age-based analysis is US-only too, purely because of recruitment constraints.
And it's one domain, retail customer service?

Single domain, tau-Bench retail specifically. They flag healthcare as a place where longer interactions and more cultural variation could make these effects bigger, not smaller, but that's a hypothesis for someone else to test, not something they showed.
And the agent itself was held fixed the whole time, GPT-4o only.

Deliberately, to isolate the user-simulation effect cleanly. Fair methodological call, but it means they can't say whether a weaker or stronger agent shows the same calibration gaps. That's punted to future work.
Here's my real question, and it's about strategy, not scope. Is building a better simulator even the right goal, or are we chasing a number that can't be fixed that way?
You mean fixable in principle versus worth fixing in practice?
Right. Even if you could theoretically tune a simulator to match real humans, maybe the effort belongs somewhere else, like just requiring real users for anything that ships.

Fair distinction, and there's a data point in the appendix that argues against easy optimism on the tuning side. They told the simulated user to dial back the politeness and reran an eighteen-task subset.
Did it actually help?

Mixed. Eleven of eighteen tasks shifted difficulty bins from one prompt tweak, overall success dropped from 50 to 46.7 percent, and calibration improved for AAVE, Indian, and Kenyan participants, but got worse for Standard American English and Nigerian participants.
So patching the prompt doesn't converge on fair, it just relocates the unfairness.

Which is exactly why their real recommendation is transparency and multi-model checks rather than a hunt for one perfectly calibrated simulator. Doesn't that undercut the whole premise that better simulation is the fix?

It does, a little. Before we wrap, though, credit where it's due on the ethics side. Compensation wasn't adjusted by country, participants were told the procedure upfront and could withdraw anytime, and the study is classified minimal risk.

And they're honest about the stakes past the study room. If simulated users get treated as a stand-in for real evaluation, some demographic groups could end up quietly underserved by whatever actually ships.
Let's close the loop, then. The paper is Lost in Simulation, LLM-Simulated Users are Unreliable Proxies for Human Users in Agentic Evaluations, Seshadri and colleagues.

And the headline holds up even though the details are messy. Robustness cracked across simulator models, validity cracked against real human behavior, and fairness cracked worst of all, right along the lines you'd worry about.
Simulated users aren't a free substitute for people. Thanks for working through this one with us.
Thanks for listening. See you next paper.
